# Actual maximum certificate for the free-mixture selector

This is a necessary geometric system, not an existence theorem for an
OC point in the proposed set. Let d>=1 and let compatible positive
fibers A,B,C occur at -1,0,1. Put

    a=|A|<c=|C|, b=|B|, M=a+b+c,
    c<a+b, b<a+c, tau=gamma_d M/2.

Let Sigma_a(C) be the measures sigma<=1_C dx of mass a. Define

    Z_0={ (g_A+g_sigma)/2: sigma in Sigma_a(C) },
    Z=conv({g_B} union Z_0).                            (1)

The coefficient of the mixture in (1) is unrestricted. In particular
this differs from the fixed coefficient 2a/(b+2a) used in the older
selector body Y. Both Z_0 and Z are compact convex subsets of int B.
Compactness follows from weak compactness of dominated measures; the
centroid of any positive dominated submeasure of a convex body lies in
its interior. More uniformly, every midpoint here contains half of an
interior ball about g_A from A, and the compact convex hull with g_B
remains inside int B.

## 1. A common cap cannot be bad at both ends of a selected segment

For any convex body K and any submeasure sigma<=1_K dx of mass a>0,
every closed halfspace containing g_sigma has K-volume at least
gamma_d a. Here is a proof that does not assume log-concavity of sigma.
Fix a nonzero normal, put F(t)=|K intersect {u.x>=t}|, and set
G=F^(1/d). Brunn-Minkowski gives concavity of G on the projection
interval. The pushforward of uniform volume on K under x->F(u.x)
is uniform Lebesgue measure on [0,|K|], by inversion of the continuous
strictly decreasing cap distribution. Thus the corresponding pushforward
of sigma is dominated by that interval's Lebesgue measure. Among such
measures of mass a, the integral of the increasing function s^(1/d)
is minimized by uniform measure on [0,a]. Jensen consequently gives

    F(u.g_sigma)^(1/d)
       >=(1/a) integral F(u.x)^(1/d) d sigma(x)
       >=(d/(d+1))a^(1/d).

Raising to the d-th power proves the assertion. Enlarging a through-point
halfspace only increases its volume.

For any m=(g_A+g_sigma)/2 in Z_0, an ambient halfspace containing (0,m)
contains at least one of (-1,g_A) and (1,g_sigma), since its affine
margin at the midpoint is the mean of the two endpoint margins. The
preceding result and ordinary Grunbaum therefore give endpoint mass
at least gamma_d a. If this same cap also contains (0,g_B), its middle
mass is at least gamma_d b. Its total mass is then at least

    gamma_d(a+b)>gamma_d(a+b+c)/2=tau.                  (2)

This applies to vertical caps as well: at least one endpoint is then
entirely present. Consequently EVERY cap of mass below tau containing
g_B excludes ALL of Z_0, and every such cap containing any m in Z_0
excludes g_B. Exclusion is strict in its affine margin because the caps
are closed.

If g_B belongs to Z_0, (2) already proves the desired bound at g_B.
Thus a putative strict failure throughout Z necessarily has g_B outside
Z_0.

## 2. An actual maximum cannot occur at the two endpoint sets

Let f(y) be the original unnormalized mixed depth of (0,y), as in
`candidate dcde24475c7f190c`. It is continuous
near Z, and every nonvertical minimum cap is attained in a compact
normal family. Suppose

    D=max_(y in Z) f(y)<tau.

Then no maximizer lies in {g_B} union Z_0.

To verify the strict statement, first take y=g_B and any fixed m in Z_0.
Every active cap at y has mass below tau and therefore its continuous
normal u satisfies u.(m-y)<0 by (2). This strict inequality is uniform
over the compact active cap family. It remains uniform over a sufficiently
small neighborhood of that active family. Translating the center a small
distance toward m lowers every such cap threshold uniformly; its central
section has a positive uniform lower volume bound because y is interior
to B. Hence all these cap masses increase by at least a fixed positive
multiple of the center displacement. The other caps have a uniform
positive mass gap above f(y) and retain it for small displacements by
uniform continuity. Thus f strictly increases toward m. The same proof
at any m in Z_0 uses the direction g_B-m. The proof retains supporting
endpoint facets: their volume changes have the same nondecreasing sign,
while the proper middle section supplies the strict increase.

Every maximizing y_* therefore has a representation

    y_*=(1-t)g_B+t m_*,  m_* in Z_0, 0<t<1.            (3)

This holds for every representation of y_* in (1), since either t=0
or t=1 would put it in an excluded endpoint set.

## 3. Actual active caps and the additional radial equality

The compact marginal-gradient proof in sections 2-5 of
`candidate dcde24475c7f190c` applies to any
compact convex constraint set inside int B. Apply it to Z. There are
k<=d+1 actual caps of mass D through (0,y_*), with unit continuous
normals u_j, integer coefficients v_j, positive weights omega_j summing
to one, and consistent effective section measures satisfying

    S_j,-1=S_j,1,
    sum_z X_jz=S_j y_*,   S_j=sum_z S_jz>0.

The vector u_bar=sum_j omega_j S_j u_j minimizes its linear functional
over Z at y_*. In (3), linearity and 0<t<1 force

    u_bar.g_B=u_bar.m_*=u_bar.y_*=min_(y in Z)u_bar.y.    (4)

Thus the new radial equality is

    u_bar.(m_*-g_B)=0.                                  (5)

If u_bar!=0, minimization over Z_0 uniquely selects the uniform lower
a-volume cap C' of C in that normal. Consequently

    m_*=(g_A+g_C')/2,
    u_bar.(g_A+g_C'-2g_B)=0.                            (6)

If u_bar=0, there is instead a positive section-weighted normal balance;
an indicator selector is not asserted. Equations (4)-(6) use actual
minimum caps and the same section traces as their zero integer/angular
derivatives. They do not invoke a shifted cap cover.

The full effective section of each cap also has depth at least
gamma_(d-1)/2 at its anchor, by section 7 of that same note.

## 4. A planar restriction on the nonzero-normal branch

Each nonzero supporting normal of Z_0 has a unique minimizing point:
the corresponding volume-a lower cap of C is unique almost everywhere,
by the strict scalar projection distribution and the elementary bathtub
inequality. Thus Z_0 is strictly convex. It has nonempty interior because
0<a<c: small swaps of positive density between disjoint interior balls
of C allow its moment to vary in every coordinate direction.

For d=2 and g_B outside Z_0 there are exactly two supporting lines of
Z_0 that pass through g_B. One way to see this is to consider the set
of directions of rays from g_B meeting the compact convex set Z_0;
it is a closed angular interval of length strictly below pi. Its two
extreme rays are the two tangents, with unique contact points by strict
convexity. Every other supporting line through g_B would supply a
different extreme ray, which is impossible.

Thus any maximum in (3) with u_bar!=0 lies on one of the two tangent
segments joining g_B to these two determined contact points of Z_0.
The branch u_bar=0 remains possible, including an interior maximum.
For d=1 every maximum is interior to the interval Z, so only this
balanced branch occurs.

These are structural necessary conditions. Neither they nor the numerical
screens establish that the free-mixture set Z always contains an OC point.
